title: A Coming Day of Judgment
overview: Zephaniah announces that a day of judgment is coming on Judah and Jerusalem for mixing the worship of other gods with the LORD and for comfortable indifference.

parts.label: Who and when (v. 1)
parts.note: Zephaniah spoke during the reign of Josiah, a king of Judah in the late 600s BC who led a push to remove idol worship, though it is unclear whether Zephaniah spoke before, during or after that reform. His family line is traced back four generations to a Hezekiah, possibly the earlier king of that name, but scholars are not certain.

parts.label: Sweeping everything away (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: The LORD threatens to wipe out people, animals, birds and fish, which echoes the flood story in Genesis. Most readers take this as vivid language for total ruin, aimed especially at the idols that lead people astray.

parts.label: Divided worship in Judah (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: The focus narrows to Jerusalem: the worship of Baal, a Canaanite storm god, idol priests, people praying to the stars on their flat rooftops, and people who swear by the LORD and also by Molek, a god linked with child sacrifice. Those who have simply drifted away and no longer seek the LORD are condemned too.

parts.label: A grim sacrifice (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: The coming day is pictured as a sacrifice in which Judah itself is the victim, and the invited guests are often understood as an invading army. Officials, royal princes and those copying foreign dress and customs are named, along with people who fill a house with violence and fraud, though the meaning of the threshold custom in verse 9 is unclear.

parts.label: Wailing across the city (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: Cries rise from the Fish Gate, a newer district and the market where traders work, and some interpreters read this order as an enemy moving deeper into Jerusalem. The LORD will search the city as if with lamps for people as sluggish as wine left sitting on its sediment, so comfortable they think God does nothing at all, and their houses and vineyards will be lost.

parts.label: A day of darkness (vv. 14-18)
parts.note: The day is described with piled up words of gloom, war trumpets and attacks on fortified towns, and the violence is stated bluntly, with blood poured out like dust and silver and gold unable to buy safety. Many read this as pointing to Babylon's conquest of Jerusalem a few decades later, while the language about the whole earth reaches beyond that event.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this day of the LORD describes only Judah's fall to Babylon or also looks ahead to a final worldwide judgment at the end of history.
think: What makes a person stop expecting that anything they do will lead to consequences, good or bad?
